title: Looping in Interesting Ways
summary: Skip elements, walk backwards, reverse in place, filter into new slices, and compare neighbors.
intro: A plain loop visits every element once from front to back. Small changes to the loop header or body give you the shapes you will use again and again: stepping by 2, counting down, meeting in the middle, collecting matches, and looking at the element before.

steps.title: Skipping elements

example.title: Even positions and odd values
example.prompt: Print the elements at even indexes, then only the odd values, one per line.
example.explanation: The first loop starts at 0 and adds 2 each pass, so it reads indexes 0, 2, 4 and 6. Index 8 fails `i < len(nums)` and the loop ends. The second loop visits every value, and `continue` skips the even ones before they reach `fmt.Println`.

practice.title: Odd positions and multiples of 3
practice.prompt:
Print the letters at odd indexes, then only the numbers that are multiples of 3, one per line.

1. Below `Odd indexes:`, loop over `letters` starting at index 1 and stepping by 2, printing each letter.
2. Below `Multiples of 3:`, range over `nums` and use `continue` to skip any number where `n%3` is not 0.
3. Print each number you keep on its own line.
4. Remove the `_ =` lines once you use the slices.

Expected output:

```text
Odd indexes:
b
d
f
Multiples of 3:
9
12
15
```

tests.output:
Odd indexes:
b
d
f
Multiples of 3:
9
12
15

hints: Copy the first loop of the example, but start `i` at 1 and loop over `letters`.
Inside the range loop, `if n%3 != 0 { continue }` skips the numbers you do not want.

steps.title: Walking backwards and reversing

example.title: Backwards words and reversed numbers
example.prompt: Print a slice of words backwards, then reverse a slice of numbers in place and print it.
example.explanation: The first loop starts at index 3 and counts down to 0. The second loop swaps positions 0 and 4, then 1 and 3. Then `i` and `j` both reach 2, `i < j` is false, and the middle 3 stays where it is. `fmt.Println(nums)` shows the same slice, now in reverse order.

practice.title: Backwards days and reversed scores
practice.prompt:
Print the days backwards, then reverse the scores in place.

1. Loop over `days` from the last index down to 0, printing each day on its own line.
2. Reverse `scores` in place with a two-index loop and a swap.
3. Keep the given `fmt.Println(scores)` line after the loop.
4. Remove the `_ = days` line once you use the slice.

Expected output:

```text
Wed
Tue
Mon
[3 5 7 9]
```
hints: Count down from `len(days) - 1` and keep going while `i >= 0`.
For the reverse, start `i` at 0 and `j` at the last index, and stop when they meet with `i < j`.
Swap each pair with one multiple assignment, no temporary variable needed.

steps.title: Filtering into a new slice

example.title: Passed and failed scores
example.prompt: Split scores into passed (60 or more) and failed, collect perfect scores, and report when there are none.
example.output:
Passed: [82 67 90 71]
Failed: [45 38]
No perfect scores
All: [45 82 67 90 38 71]
example.explanation: Each score goes into exactly one of `passed` or `failed` through the if/else, and the separate `if` collects perfect scores. No score is 100, so `perfect` is still nil and `len(perfect) == 0` prints the message. `passed` started as `[]int{}` and `failed` as nil, yet both print the same way. The last line shows `scores` was never modified.

practice.title: Above zero and freezing
practice.prompt:
Split temperatures into above zero and freezing, collect boiling ones, and report when there are none.

1. Range over `temps` and append each value above 0 to `above`, and every other value to `freezing`.
2. In the same loop, also append any value of 100 or more to `boiling`.
3. After the `Freezing:` line, print `None boiling` when `boiling` has length 0, otherwise print `Boiling:` followed by the slice.
4. Keep the other `fmt.Println` lines as given, and remove the `_ = boiling` line once you use the slice.

Expected output:

```text
Above: [5 12 7]
Freezing: [-3 0 -8]
None boiling
All: [-3 5 0 12 -8 7]
```
hints: Use an if/else for above and freezing, then a separate `if` for boiling.
Grow a slice with `above = append(above, t)`.
Check for no matches with `if len(boiling) == 0 {`.

steps.title: Comparing neighbors
steps.body:
Many questions are about how a value changes from one element to the next. Start the loop at 1 and compare `s[i]` with the element before it, `s[i-1]`.

```go harness
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	s := []int{100, 104, 101, 107, 107, 110}
	{{code}}
}
```

```go
for i := 1; i < len(s); i++ {
	change := s[i] - s[i-1]
	fmt.Println(change)
}
```

Starting at 1 matters: at `i := 0` the expression `s[i-1]` reads index -1 and panics. A slice of length n has n - 1 neighbor pairs, so this loop runs one time fewer than the length, and not at all when the slice has fewer than 2 elements.

The sign of each difference tells you the direction. Count rises with `change > 0` and drops with `change < 0`. A change of 0 is neither, so it lands in no count.

To print a change with its sign, use the `+` flag. `%+d` always prints a sign, so positive numbers get a `+` and zero prints as `+0`.

```go
fmt.Printf("%+d\n", 4)  // +4
fmt.Printf("%+d\n", -3) // -3
```

example.title: Daily price changes
example.prompt: Print each day-to-day price change with its sign, then count the days the price went up.
example.explanation: The loop starts at index 1, so every pass has a previous day to compare with. Six prices give five changes. `%+d` adds the `+` to the rises and to the flat day, which prints `+0` and is not counted. Three changes are above 0, so `upDays` ends at 3.

practice.title: Lap time changes
practice.prompt:
Print each lap-to-lap time change with its sign, then count the laps that were faster than the one before.

1. Loop over `laps` starting at index 1.
2. Compute the change as the current lap minus the previous lap and print it with `%+d`, one per line.
3. A faster lap has a lower time, so add 1 to `faster` when the change is below 0.
4. Remove the `_ = laps` line and keep the final `fmt.Println` line.

Expected output:

```text
-2
+1
-3
+0
Faster laps: 2
```
hints: Start at index 1 so `laps[i-1]` always exists.
The change is `laps[i] - laps[i-1]`, and a negative change means a faster lap.
Print it with `fmt.Printf` and the `%+d` verb, ending the format with `\n`.

recap:
- `i += 2` visits every other element. Start at 0 for even indexes and at 1 for odd ones.
- `continue` skips the rest of the body and moves to the next element.
- `for i := len(s) - 1; i >= 0; i--` walks a slice backwards.
- `for i, j := 0, len(s)-1; i < j; i, j = i+1, j-1` with `s[i], s[j] = s[j], s[i]` reverses in place.
- Filter by appending matches to a new slice. The original stays unchanged.
- Nil and empty slices both print `[]`, so test for no matches with `len(out) == 0`.
- Start at `i := 1` to compare `s[i]` with `s[i-1]`, and print signed changes with `%+d`.
